title: Stress and the accent marks
objectives: I can count the syllables of a word and find its stressed syllable, and I know the terms oxytone, paroxytone and proparoxytone.
I can apply the default stress rule to the ending of a word and decide whether a written accent is needed.
I can explain what the acute, circumflex, tilde, cedilla and grave marks each do.
I can explain, step by step, why words such as você, café, avó, avô, português, ônibus, está and pôde are written as they are.
I can predict how an accent appears, disappears or stays when a word changes to the plural, the feminine or another verb form, and I know the main writing conventions of the 2009 spelling agreement.

vocabulary.note: Two syllables: ca-sa. The word ends in a, so the default stress is on the second to last syllable: CA-sa. The actual stress matches the default, so no accent is written. The s between two vowels sounds like z: KAH-zuh.

Two syllables: a-QUI, stressed on the last. The word ends in i, and the default for i is the last syllable, so no accent is needed even though the stress is on the last syllable. The qu is a k sound with a silent u: ah-KEE.

Two syllables: fa-LAR. The word ends in r, and the default for r is the last syllable, so the stress is on the last syllable with no accent. The infinitive is the base, dictionary form of a verb, and every infinitive ending in ar, er or ir is stressed this way.

Two syllables: LÁ-pis. The word ends in is, and the default for is is the last syllable. The stress is on the first syllable, so the word breaks the default and the acute accent marks the stressed vowel. The á is open: LAH-peess. The word is the same for one pencil or several.

Two syllables: ca-FÉ. The word ends in e, so the default would be CA-fe. The stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default, so an accent is required. The e is open, like the e in bed, so the mark is the acute: é.

Historically a contraction of vossa mercê, literally your grace, a respectful way to address a person. Two syllables: vo-CÊ. The word ends in e, so the default would be VO-ce. The stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default, so an accent is required. The e is closed, like the ay in say held steady, so the mark is the circumflex: ê. Without the accent, voce would be read VO-see.
Two syllables: a-VÓ. The word ends in o, so the default would be A-vo. The stress is on the last syllable, so an accent is required. The o is open, like the aw in law, so the mark is the acute: ó.

The same letters and the same stress as avó, but the o is closed, like the o in go without the w glide, so the mark is the circumflex: ô. Only the accent tells the two words apart, and it also tells masculine from feminine.

Three syllables: por-tu-GUÊS. The word ends in es, so the default would be por-TU-gues. The stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default, so an accent is required. The e is closed, so the mark is the circumflex. The feminine form portuguesa follows the default, so the accent disappears. The name of a language is written with a lowercase letter.

Three syllables: Ô-ni-bus. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so this is a proparoxytone, and every proparoxytone is written with an accent. The o is closed, so the mark is the circumflex: O-nee-boos.

Three syllables: MÉ-di-co, a proparoxytone, so the accent is required. The e is open, so the mark is the acute. The d before i sounds like j in jeep in most of Brazil: MEH-jee-koo. The feminine form is médica, with the same accent.

Three syllables: ÁR-vo-re, a proparoxytone, so the accent is required. The a is open, so the mark is the acute. The r closes the first syllable, because rv is two different consonants and they are split: ár-vo-re.

Formed from tão bem, so well or as well, which is why it means also. Two syllables: tam-BÉM. The word ends in em, so the default would be TAM-bem. The stress is on the last syllable, so an accent is required: the acute, by convention, on a stressed e before a final m. The ending em is a nasal ay sound with no m closing the lips.

One syllable, stressed. A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o, with or without s, always takes an accent, and this one has a closed e, so the circumflex: TRÊS, with the ay of say held steady.
One syllable, stressed, ending in o, so the accent is required. The o is open, like the aw in law, so the mark is the acute: SAW.

Two syllables: a-ÇÃO. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, and the tilde already marks both the nasal sound and the stress, so no second accent is written. The cedilla makes the c sound like s before a: ah-SOWN, through the nose.

Two syllables: pa-ÍS, because a and i do not glide together and form a hiatus. The stressed í stands at the start of its syllable with only s after it, so the accent is written. Without the accent, pais is one syllable and means parents.

A form of the verb estar. With você it corresponds to English are. Two syllables: es-TÁ. The word ends in a, so the default would be ES-ta. The stress is on the last syllable, so an accent is required, with an open a: the acute. Without the accent, esta is a different word meaning this.

A form of the verb ser. One stressed syllable ending in e, so the accent is required, with an open e: EH, like the e in bed. Without the accent, e is a different word meaning and, said like the ee in see.

Two syllables: ma-ÇÃ. The ending ã is stressed on the last syllable, and the tilde marks both the nasal vowel and the stress. The cedilla makes the c sound like s before a: mah-SAH, with a nasal final vowel.

dialogues.title: Ordering at a café
dialogues.context: Ana and Bruno order from Marcos at a café counter. Look at the stress in café, você, também, três, pães and maçã, and at the accent in ótimo, a proparoxytone: Ó-ti-mo. Verb forms and small words are met whole here and explained in later lessons.

lines.target: Bom dia! O que você quer?

lines.source_literal: good day! the what you want?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.target: Eu quero um café, por favor.
lines.source_literal: I want a coffee, by favor.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.target: Eu também quero café. E três pães, por favor.
lines.source: I want coffee too. And three bread rolls, please.
lines.source_literal: I as-well want coffee. And three breads, by favor.

lines.speaker: Marcos

lines.speaker: Bruno

dialogues.title: The grandparents and the bus
dialogues.context: Lucas meets Júlia at the bus stop. Look at the stress in avó, avô, médico, ônibus, até and amanhã, and at the accent in the name Júlia. Verb forms and small words are met whole here and explained in later lessons.

lines.speaker: Júlia
lines.target: Estou, sim. Estou com a avó e o avô.
lines.source: Yes, I am. I am with my grandmother and grandfather.
lines.source_literal: I-am, yes. I-am with the grandmother and the grandfather.

lines.speaker: Júlia
lines.target: Estão. O avô é médico, e a avó também.
lines.source: They are. My grandfather is a doctor, and my grandmother is too.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.target: Que legal! E você vai de ônibus?
lines.source: How cool! And are you going by bus?
lines.source_literal: What legal! And you go of bus?

lines.speaker: Júlia
lines.target: Vou, sim. É o ônibus número três.
lines.source: Yes, I am. It is bus number three.
lines.source_literal: I-go, yes. Is the bus number three.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.source: Me too! See you tomorrow, Júlia.

dialogues.title: A day at the beach
dialogues.context: Rita and Paulo plan a trip to the beach. Look at the crase in à praia and às nove, and at the hyphen in guarda-sol. Verb forms and small words are met whole here and explained in later lessons.

lines.source: Paulo, shall we go to the beach tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.target: Tudo bem. Eu levo o guarda-sol.
lines.source: Fine. I will bring the beach umbrella.

lines.speaker: Rita

grammar.title: Syllables and stress: the terms you need
grammar.explanation:
Every spoken word is a chain of beats called syllables. A syllable is built around exactly one vowel sound, together with any consonants said in the same beat. To count the syllables of a word, count its vowel sounds: ca-sa has two, vo-cê has two, por-tu-guês has three, ô-ni-bus has three. English works the same way (ba-na-na has three), so your ear already knows how to do this.

To divide a written word into syllables, use these rules. A single consonant between two vowels goes with the vowel after it: ca-sa, a-vó, me-sa. A pair of letters that stands for one sound is never split: ch, lh, nh, and the qu and gu of que, qui, gue, gui, so you divide fi-lho, ba-nho, cha-ve. A stop or f or v followed by l or r (b, c, d, f, g, p, t, v before r; b, c, f, g, p before l) also stays together: li-vro, pra-to, pú-bli-co. Any other two consonants are split, and so are rr and ss: lin-do, es-tá, ár-vo-re, car-ro, pas-so. The same division is used when a word is broken with a hyphen at the end of a line.

A diphthong, which the lesson on sounds introduced as two vowel letters that glide into one sound (ei in lei-te, ai in pai, ão in pão, ãe in mãe), is one beat. So pai, pão and mãe each have one syllable. Two vowels that do not glide together form a hiatus and belong to two syllables: pa-ís, sa-ú-de, vo-o.

Stress is the syllable of a word that is said louder, longer and slightly higher than the others. English has it too: PHO-to-graph is stressed on the first syllable, pho-TOG-ra-phy on the second. In English you must memorize the stress of each word, and it is never written. In Portuguese the stress can be predicted from the last letters of the word (the next note), and when it cannot, the spelling marks it. Stress matters: público (PÚ-bli-co, public), publico (pu-BLI-co, I publish) and publicou (pu-bli-COU, he published) are spelled almost identically and differ in stress and meaning. In this course the stressed syllable is written in capitals.

Three technical terms come from Greek and are used in every Portuguese grammar book. A word is an oxytone if the stress is on the last syllable, a paroxytone if it is on the second to last (the penultimate) syllable, and a proparoxytone if it is on the third to last (the antepenultimate) syllable. An ordinary Portuguese word is never stressed further back than the third to last syllable. A one-syllable word is a monosyllable; some monosyllables are stressed (pé, três, pão) and some are small words that lean on their neighbor and carry no stress of their own (o, a, de, que, e).

examples.source: house. Two syllables, ca-sa, stressed on the second to last: CA-sa. A paroxytone.
coffee. Two syllables, ca-fé, stressed on the last: ca-FÉ. An oxytone.
doctor. Three syllables, mé-di-co, stressed on the third to last: MÉ-di-co. A proparoxytone.
bread. One syllable, because ão is a single nasal diphthong. A monosyllable.
country. Two syllables, pa-ís, because a and i do not glide together. An oxytone: pa-ÍS.
Portuguese. Three syllables, por-tu-guês, stressed on the last: por-tu-GUÊS. An oxytone.
public. PÚ-bli-co, a proparoxytone.
I publish. pu-BLI-co, a paroxytone. The same letters as público, with the stress moved and the accent gone.
he published. pu-bli-COU, an oxytone. Nearly the same letters again, with a final u and a third stress position.

grammar.title: The default stress rule and when an accent appears
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is designed so that most words need no stress mark. The design is a default: look at how a word ends, and the ending tells you which syllable is stressed. A reader who knows the default pronounces an unmarked word correctly. A written accent appears, in nearly every case, when a word breaks the default of its ending, and it sits on the stressed vowel. An accent is therefore never decoration: it means this word is an exception to its ending. A few accents have other reasons (the open diphthong in papéis, the hiatus in país, the differential accent in pôde), and the later notes name them.

The default has two groups. Words ending in a, e or o, with or without a final s, and words ending in am, em or ens, are stressed on the second to last syllable: CA-sa, LEI-te, LI-vro, A-mi-gos, FA-lam, HO-mem, HO-mens. These are the endings Portuguese adds to a word for gender (o and a), for the plural (s) and for the form of a verb that means they (am, em). They are added after the stem, so the stress stays where it was. Words ending in anything else are stressed on the last syllable: i or u (a-QUI, ta-TU), is or us (pa-RIS, me-NUS), l, r or z (a-NEL, fa-LAR, fe-LIZ), im, um and ns (jar-DIM, al-GUM, al-GUNS), the nasal endings ã and ão (ir-MÃ, ir-MÃO), and diphthongs such as ei, ai and ou (es-TOU).

So the procedure to write a word is: find the stressed syllable, read the default from the ending, and compare. If they agree, write no accent. If they disagree, write an accent on the stressed vowel. The next note explains which accent. Two consequences follow. First, an oxytone that ends in a, e, o, am, em or ens needs an accent (café, você, avó, também, parabéns), while an oxytone that ends in i, u, l, r or z does not (aqui, animal, falar). Second, a paroxytone that ends in i, u, is, us, l, r, n, x, z, im, um, ns, ã or ão needs an accent (lápis, vírus, fácil, açúcar, hífen, tórax, álbum, órfão).

A proparoxytone always needs an accent, because no ending predicts stress on the third to last syllable: médico, árvore, música, lâmpada. This includes words that end in a glide plus a vowel, such as ia, io, ua and uo: the spelling rule counts the i or u as a separate syllable (in speech the pair is often said as one beat), so história is his-TÓ-ri-a, stressed on the third to last, and água, família and the name Júlia are written with an accent for the same reason. A word such as tia is different: the stressed vowel is the i itself, so ti-a is a paroxytone and needs nothing.

Two further cases. A stressed monosyllable that ends in a, e or o, with or without s, takes an accent: pé, só, já, mês, três, nós. This also keeps stressed words apart from unstressed small words such as nos (us) and de (of). Other monosyllables are left unmarked: sol, mar, luz, sim, bom. Finally, a stressed i or u that is the second vowel of a hiatus is written í or ú when it is alone in its syllable or followed only by s: pa-ís, pa-í-ses, sa-ú-de, ba-ú. If l, m, n, r or z follows it in the same syllable, no accent is needed: ra-iz, ju-iz, ru-im. No accent is written either when nh follows: rai-nha, moi-nho. This accent keeps a vowel pair from being read as a diphthong: país has two syllables, pais has one.

examples.source: friend. a-MI-go. Ends in o, default second to last, actual stress second to last. They agree, so no accent.
here. a-QUI. Ends in i, default last syllable, actual stress last. They agree, so no accent.
coffee. ca-FÉ. Ends in e, default second to last, actual stress last. They disagree, so an accent.
pencil. LÁ-pis. Ends in is, default last, actual stress second to last. They disagree, so an accent.
animal. a-ni-MAL. Ends in l, default last, actual stress last. They agree, so no accent.
music. MÚ-si-ca. Stress on the third to last, a proparoxytone, so always an accent.
water. Á-gua. The ua counts as two syllables, so the stress is on the third to last, and the accent is required.
health. sa-Ú-de. A hiatus: the stressed ú is alone in its syllable, so it takes the accent.
judge. ju-IZ. A hiatus too, but the i is followed by z in its syllable, so no accent.

grammar.title: What each mark does
grammar.explanation:
A diacritic is a small mark added to a letter to say something about it. Portuguese has five. Four sit on vowels (acute, circumflex, tilde, grave) and one sits under the letter c (cedilla). They do two different jobs: some show which syllable is stressed, and some show the quality of the sound. First, two terms for vowel quality. A vowel is open when the mouth and jaw are more open, and closed when they are less open and the tongue or lips are higher or rounder.

The acute accent (acento agudo) can go on any vowel. It marks the stressed syllable of a word that breaks its default. On a, e and o it also shows that the vowel is open: á like the a in father, é like the e in bed, ó like the aw in law. The exception is before m or n, where the vowel is nasal and the mark is a convention: in the middle of a word Brazilian spelling writes the circumflex (acadêmico, Antônio, câmera), and in words ending in em or ens it writes the acute (também, parabéns). Portuguese i and u have only one quality, so í and ú only mark stress or a hiatus: a-ÇÚ-car, sa-Í-da.

The circumflex (acento circunflexo) goes only on a, e and o. It marks stress and shows that the vowel is closed: ê like the ay in say held steady, ô like the o in go without the w glide, â a more closed central a, nearer to the weak final a of casa than to the open a of father. The â is found mostly where a stressed a is followed by m or n: câmera (camera), lâmpada (lamp). So acute and circumflex differ in the sound, and you learn which one a word has together with the word. Pairs such as avó and avô, where only the mark differs, show how much work the mark does.

What if a stressed e or o has no mark at all, as in mesa or festa? The default rule fixes the stressed syllable, not the quality of its vowel. Mesa has a closed e and festa an open e; nome has a closed o and porta an open o. Listen and remember the word. The marks cover only the exceptions.

The tilde (til) goes only on a and o and makes the vowel nasal, meaning air flows through the nose: ã, õ, and the nasal diphthongs ão, ãe, õe. It has a second job: unless the word already has an acute or circumflex, the tilde also marks the stressed syllable, which is why irmã, irmão, maçã, amanhã, pães and limões need nothing more. When another accent is present, the accent shows the stress and the tilde only shows the nasal sound: órfão is ÓR-fão.

The cedilla (cedilha) exists for one reason. The letter c sounds like k before a, o and u (casa, copo, cuba) and like s before e and i (cedo, cinco). To write an s sound before a, o or u, Portuguese puts a cedilla under the c: ça, ço, çu are sa, so, su. So ç never appears before e or i, and never at the start of a word. It has no effect on stress: ca-BE-ça, a-ÇÃO.

The grave accent (acento grave) has exactly one use, called crase, from a Greek word for blending. Two small words are involved. The preposition a is a small word that links a verb to its destination or time and means to or at. The article a is the word for the before feminine words, and its plural is as. When the preposition a meets the article a, they fuse into one long a, written à, and with as they fuse into às. The grave only records the fusion. It does not mark stress and does not open the vowel. A practical test: replace the feminine word by a masculine one. If you would say ao (the preposition a fused with the article o), the feminine word takes à: Vou ao mercado, Vou à praia. Where there is no article, there is no fusion and no accent: A que horas?

rows: stress; on a, e, o also an open vowel
a nasal vowel; also the stress when no other accent is present
c sounds like s before a, o, u
crase: the fusion of the preposition a and the article a

examples.source: coffee. Acute: stress on the last syllable and an open é.
you. Circumflex: stress on the last syllable and a closed ê.
camera. Circumflex on â: a stressed a before m, closed and nasal.
sister. Tilde: a nasal ã, and the tilde also marks the stress on the last syllable, so no second accent.
orphan. The acute marks the stress on the first syllable; the tilde here only marks the nasal sound.
head. Cedilla: the ç sounds like s before a. The stress is the default, second to last.
I go to the beach. à is the preposition a fused with the article a before the feminine word praia.
I go to the market. With a masculine word the fusion is ao, so no accent.
At nine o'clock. às is the preposition a fused with the plural article as.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: first-contact words
grammar.explanation:
This note applies the two previous notes to the words you meet first, one step at a time. The method is always the same. First, divide the word into syllables. Second, find the stressed syllable by ear. Third, read the default from the ending. Fourth, if the stress disagrees with the default, the stressed vowel needs an accent, and you choose acute or circumflex by the quality of the vowel, open or closed.

Take você, the word that puzzles most beginners. It divides into vo-cê. The stress is on the last syllable. The ending is e, and the default for e is the second to last syllable, which would give VO-ce. The stress disagrees with the default, so an accent is required on the stressed vowel. The vowel is closed, like the ay in say held steady, so the accent is the circumflex: ê. Café follows the same steps with an open e, so it takes the acute. Avó and avô are a-VÓ and a-VÔ: the ending o would default to A-vo, the stress is on the last syllable, and the vowel quality chooses the mark: open ó for the grandmother, closed ô for the grandfather. Português is por-tu-GUÊS: the ending es defaults to the second to last, the stress is on the last, and the closed e takes the circumflex. Também is tam-BÉM: the ending em defaults to TAM-bem, so the stress on the last syllable needs an accent.

The proparoxytones ônibus, médico, público and árvore are stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so they always carry an accent. The vowel quality decides the mark: closed o gives ô, open e gives é, open a gives á, and u, which has only one quality, takes the acute. Três, só and pé are stressed one-syllable words ending in e or o (with or without s), which always take an accent, and the vowel quality again decides the mark. Ação is a-ÇÃO: the ending ão defaults to the last syllable, so the tilde alone is enough, and the cedilla records that c sounds like s before a. Pães has one syllable: the nasal diphthong ãe, and the tilde marks both the nasal sound and the stress.

Some pairs differ only by an accent. In é and e, é is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it needs the accent (EH, open, meaning is), while e is an unstressed small word said like the ee of see, meaning and. In está and esta, está is es-TÁ with the stress on the last syllable, breaking the default of a, while esta is ES-ta, following the default (this, before a feminine word). In país and pais, the accent shows two syllables instead of one and changes the meaning from parents to country. In avó and avô, the mark alone separates the grandmother from the grandfather.

A few accents are different, because the default rule does not predict them. Pode (he can) and pôde (he could, on one occasion) are both stressed on the first syllable and end in e, so by the default rule neither needs a mark. The circumflex on pôde shows a closed o and exists only to tell the two words apart: PÓ-de with an open o, PÔ-de with a closed o. Por is a small unstressed word meaning by, for or through, and pôr is the stressed infinitive to put. By the default for r, pôr would need no accent, so its circumflex is again only there to tell it from por. Accents that only tell words apart are called differential accents, and the 2009 spelling agreement left very few, including pôde, pôr, and têm and vêm (met in a later note). Para (to, for; also he stops) used to be pára when it meant he stops, and the mark was removed, so context now decides.

examples.source: You are here. Both você and está break the default of their endings and carry an accent.
This house is lovely. esta, without an accent, means this and is stressed on the first syllable.
Coffee and bread. The é in café is open and stressed; the e meaning and is unstressed and has no accent.
The grandfather and the grandmother. The closed ô is masculine and the open ó is feminine.
She can speak Portuguese. pode is the present, with an open o.
She could not speak, on that occasion. pôde is the past, with a closed o.

examples.target: Eu quero pôr o café aqui.
examples.source: I want to put the coffee here. pôr is the infinitive to put.
Let's go this way. por is the small unstressed word meaning by or through.
The country is lovely. país has two syllables, pa-ÍS.
The parents are here. pais has one syllable and no accent.

grammar.title: Accents that appear, disappear and move
grammar.explanation:
An accent belongs to one form of a word, not to the whole family of forms. Every time a word changes its ending, the default for the new ending may be different, so you recompute: find the stress, read the default, compare. There are three possible results. The accent stays, because the new form still breaks its default. The accent disappears, because the new form now agrees with its default. Or an accent appears, because the new form now breaks its default.

The changes seen most often are these. The plural (meaning more than one) usually adds s or es. Gender is the grouping of nouns into masculine and feminine; many words for people and nationalities change their ending to show it, for example o and a (the next lesson explains gender in full). A verb form is the shape a verb takes to say who does the action; the infinitive is the base form that ends in ar, er or ir, and the infinitive estar, to be, gives está (he, she or it is, or you are) and estão (they are). The accent follows the ending in every case.

Accents stay when the stress and the break are unchanged: país and países keep the í because it is still alone in its syllable, café and avó keep their marks in cafés and avós, and você keeps its circumflex in vocês, because the ending es would default to the second to last and the stress is still on the last. Accents disappear when the longer form matches the default: mês becomes meses (ME-ses, stressed on the second to last, as es defaults), francês becomes francesa (fran-CE-sa, where a defaults to the second to last, although the e is still closed), and português becomes portuguesa. Accents appear when a plain oxytone takes a new ending: papel ends in l, so it needs none, but its plural papéis has an open stressed e in the diphthong ei, and Portuguese writes the acute on the open diphthongs éi, éu and ói when they are stressed on the last syllable (papéis, céu, herói), to show the open vowel. The ending ais does not need one: animal becomes animais.

Some words need no accent either before or after. Ele and eles are both stressed on the first syllable, as e and es default, and homem and homens are both stressed on the first syllable, as em and ens default. The tilde and the acute can swap: está, with an acute because it ends in a, has the plural form estão, in which ão defaults to the last syllable and the tilde alone marks the nasal sound and the stress. Finally, the circumflex can mark a plural in writing: tem (he has) and têm (they have), vem (he comes) and vêm (they come) are different in writing only, because in Brazilian Portuguese they sound the same.

examples.source: The country is lovely.
The countries are lovely. The í stays.
He is French. fran-CÊS keeps its circumflex.
She is French. fran-CE-sa needs no accent.
They are French. fran-CE-ses needs no accent either.
Three months. mês became meses, and the accent is gone.
You all are here. vocês keeps its circumflex; estão has a tilde where está has an acute.
He has coffee. tem has no accent.
They have coffee. têm has a circumflex, which is written but not heard.

grammar.title: Writing conventions and the 2009 spelling agreement
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese capitalizes less than English. A capital letter is used for the first word of a sentence and for the names of people, places and institutions: Ana, Brasil, São Paulo. A title capitalizes only its first word and its proper names. Lowercase is used where English uses a capital: the pronoun eu (I), the names of languages (português, inglês), words for nationalities (brasileiro, francesa), the days of the week and the months, and forms of address such as senhor and dona.

Question marks and exclamation marks come only at the end of the sentence, as in English. There is no inverted mark at the start, unlike Spanish. A question often has the same word order as a statement, and the mark and the rising intonation are the only signals: Você está aqui. is a statement and Você está aqui? is a question. Commas and periods work as in English, with one difference in numbers: Portuguese writes a comma for the decimal point and a period to group thousands, so 3,50 is three and a half and 1.000 is one thousand.

The hyphen joins the parts of some compound words: guarda-sol (beach umbrella), guarda-chuva (umbrella), segunda-feira (Monday), bem-vindo (welcome). It also joins some prefixes to a word, such as micro-ondas (microwave), where two identical vowels meet, and in formal writing it joins a pronoun to a verb. Each part of a hyphenated compound keeps its own stress marks, as in água-viva (jellyfish). A hyphen also marks the division of a word at the end of a line, by the syllable rules of the first note.

The 2009 spelling agreement (Acordo Ortográfico) simplified several rules, and it is in force in Brazil (mandatory since 2016). The trema, the two dots over u in gue, gui, que and qui, was abolished. The u is still pronounced in those words, so the words must be learned: linguiça (lin-GUI-ça), frequência (fre-QUÊN-cia, with a kw sound), tranquilo, cinquenta and pinguim. In most other words the u is silent, as in queijo and guerra. The acute accent was removed from the open ei and oi diphthongs of paroxytones: ideia, heroico, jiboia, assembleia, geleia. It stays on oxytones and monosyllables: papéis, herói, céu, dói. The circumflex was removed in paroxytones ending in oo and ee: voo, enjoo, abençoo, veem, leem, creem. The acute was removed from an i or u after a diphthong in a paroxytone: feiura. Most differential accents were removed: para (was pára), pera (was pêra), pelo (was pêlo), polo (was pólo); pôde, pôr, têm and vêm survive. The letters k, w and y officially joined the alphabet. Brazilian spelling had already dropped silent consonants that European spelling kept until 2009: fato, ótimo, coleção.

rows: trema removed; the u is still pronounced
trema removed; the u is still pronounced
acute removed from the open ei of a paroxytone
acute removed from the open oi of a paroxytone
acute removed from an i after a diphthong

examples.source: I speak Portuguese and English. Languages and eu are lowercase.
Are you here? The question mark is only at the end.
How cool! The exclamation mark is only at the end.
The idea is good. Since 2009, ideia has no accent.
The flight is at nine. Since 2009, voo has no circumflex.
The sausage is here. There is no trema, but the u is pronounced: lin-GUI-ça.
They see the tree. Since 2009, veem has no circumflex.
I bring the umbrella. The hyphen joins the two parts of the compound.

culture.title: Accents in everyday Brazilian life
culture.text:
In quick text messages Brazilians often leave out accents and cedillas and write voce, nao or acucar. Readers decode these without trouble, because context supplies the missing information. Formal writing is different. School essays, university entrance exams, official documents and job applications are expected to be correctly accented, and a missing mark can change a word: sabia and sábia, publico and público, pais and país are different words. Dictation exercises, the ditado, are a familiar part of school life in Brazil, and children learn the terms oxítona, paroxítona and proparoxítona in primary school when they study the regras de acentuação, the accent rules. The terms you have learned in this lesson are the same ones you will find in any Brazilian grammar book or on a Brazilian educational website.

The spelling agreement of 2009 was part of a long effort to give the Portuguese-speaking countries one written standard. Pronunciation still differs between Brazil, Portugal, Angola and Mozambique, and a few words keep two accepted spellings, but the written language is now far more uniform than it was. Brazilian keyboards of the standard ABNT2 layout have a dedicated key for ç, and the accents are typed as a dead key followed by the vowel, so Brazilians write them without thinking about it. If your own keyboard has no such key, learn how to type the accented letters now, because a correct accent is part of spelling a word, not decoration.

exercises.prompt: How many syllables does the word 'português' have?
exercises.explanation: por-tu-guês. The gu before ê is one sound, and each of the three syllables has one vowel sound.

exercises.prompt: Which of these words is an oxytone, stressed on the last syllable?
exercises.explanation: ca-FÉ is stressed on the last syllable. CA-sa and LI-vro are paroxytones, and MÉ-di-co is a proparoxytone.

exercises.prompt: The word 'livro' ends in o. Where does the default rule put the stress?
choices: On the third to last syllable
On the second to last syllable
exercises.explanation: Words ending in a, e or o are stressed on the second to last syllable: LI-vro.

exercises.hint_source: I want a coffee. Stress on the last syllable, with an open e.
exercises.explanation: The word ends in e, whose default is the second to last syllable, but the stress is on the last. It needs an accent, and the open e takes the acute: café.

exercises.prompt: What does the circumflex in 'avô' tell you?
choices: A closed o, and the stress
An open o, and the stress
An o that sounds like s
exercises.explanation: The circumflex marks the stress and a closed vowel. The open vowel of avó is written with the acute.

exercises.hint_source: Are you here? Add the missing letter with its accent.
exercises.explanation: You is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for e, and the e is closed, so it takes the circumflex: você.

exercises.prompt: The word 'aqui' is stressed on the last syllable. Why does it need no accent?
choices: Because it has only two syllables
Because words ending in i are stressed on the last syllable by default
exercises.explanation: An accent appears only when the stress breaks the default of the ending. For i, the default is the last syllable.
Está, with the acute, is the verb. Esta, without an accent, means this.
Café and está both break the default of their endings, so both carry an acute.
The preposition a fuses with the feminine article a of praia: a plus a is à, which is called crase.

exercises.prompt: What is the only use of the grave accent in Portuguese?
choices: Marking the fusion of the preposition a with the feminine article a
exercises.explanation: The grave accent writes the fusion called crase: a plus a is à, and a plus as is às. It does not change the stress.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with the position of its stress

exercises.hint_source: Do you want coffee? Two words carry an accent.
I want an apple. The missing letters are a c with a cedilla and an a with a tilde.
exercises.explanation: The cedilla makes the c sound like s before a, and the ending ã is stressed on the last syllable, marked by the tilde.

exercises.prompt: Which syllable is stressed in computador, com-pu-ta-dor? The word is written with no accent.
exercises.explanation: The word ends in r, whose default is the last syllable: com-pu-ta-DOR. No accent is needed.
Também needs its acute because the stress on the last syllable breaks the default for em.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'lápis' need an accent while 'casa' does not?
choices: Lápis is a longer word than casa
Lápis ends in is, whose default is the last syllable, but it is stressed on the first
exercises.explanation: Casa is stressed where its ending predicts. Lápis is not, so the accent marks the exception.
Estão is the form of estar used with eles. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, and the tilde marks the nasal sound and the stress.

exercises.prompt: Pode and pôde are both stressed on the first syllable. Why does pôde have a circumflex?
choices: It makes the word stressed on the last syllable
It tells pôde, the past with a closed o, apart from pode, the present with an open o
exercises.explanation: This is a differential accent: it is not predicted by the default rule, and it exists only to separate two words.

exercises.hint_source: The tree is here. The stress is on the first of three syllables.
exercises.explanation: The stress is on the third to last syllable, so the word is a proparoxytone and always takes an accent. The open a takes the acute.

exercises.prompt: Francês has an accent but francesa does not. Why?
choices: The accent moves to the a
Fran-CE-sa ends in a, so the stress on the second to last syllable is the default and needs no mark
exercises.explanation: The accent belongs to the form. The new ending agrees with its default, so the accent disappears, and the e is still closed.

exercises.prompt: Which spelling follows the 2009 spelling agreement?
exercises.explanation: The acute was removed from the open ei of paroxytones. It stays in oxytones and monosyllables, such as herói and papéis.
The grave accent writes the fusion of the preposition a and the article a of praia.

exercises.hint_source: The doctor is here too. Three words carry an accent.

exercises.prompt: Match each example with the mark it shows
Anel, ring, is stressed on the last syllable: a-NEL. Does it need an accent?
choices: No, because words ending in l are stressed on the last syllable by default
exercises.explanation: The stress agrees with the default of l, so no accent is written. Only a disagreement with the default needs a mark.
Both também and café break the default of their endings, so both carry an acute.

exercises.hint_source: Let's go to the beach at nine. The grave accent appears twice.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between pais and país?
choices: They are the same word with two spellings
Pais is one syllable meaning parents, and país has two syllables, stressed on the í, meaning country
Pais means country and país means parents
exercises.explanation: The accent shows that the a and the i are in different syllables, which also changes the stress and the meaning.
Avó has an open ó, and está breaks the default of a.
